segments.text: Hello and welcome to this week's Health Report with me, Norman Swan. Today, a warning about a potentially dangerous drug interaction that some people with what's called atrial fibrillation might have.
Success in Western Australia at reducing the rate of preterm births, but it's hard work. A calculator for success with IVF.
And the media who have been full of the thunderstorm asthma event in Melbourne two weeks ago.
Thousands of people turning up in emergency departments, intensive care admissions and several deaths.
One reason for the impact is thought to be that too many people with asthma don't recognise that their condition is worse than it is and are on the wrong treatment.
Basically, throughout Australia, there's a cohort of people who live with unacceptable asthma symptoms.
Someone who studied this is Matthew Peters, who's Professor of Respiratory Medicine at Macquarie University in Sydney.
Welcome to The Health Report.
Good evening, Norman.
I should just say that Matthew's speaking to us by Skype from Vienna, where he's at a conference.
Just before we get to this unacceptable level of symptoms in the community,
what do we know about the causes of this huge event?
Is it simply pollen?
It's a combination of circumstances, including pollen.
You need a buildup of pollen.
So typically in Australia, it's grass pollen because that's carried on breezes.
So a number of days of pollen buildup and then preceding the thunderstorm,
typically there are winds and downdrafts.
They take the pollen up into the cloud base
and simply because there's distilled water,
the larger pollen particles are broken up
into much smaller pollen particles
and the smaller ones are then dispersed in the storm.
And these smaller ones are of a sufficiently small calibre
to penetrate deep into the airways and establish an asthma reaction.
And it's a true asthma reaction?
Oh, no question. And probably electrical forces contribute as well. It's a very complex milieu.
So tell us about this group of people with unacceptable asthma symptoms.
And what asthma symptoms are we talking about here?
We're talking about wheeze, breathlessness, chest tightness, general incapacity to consistently go around your tasks of daily life without breathlessness.
the ones we worry most about are those which are disturbing during the
small hours of the morning or on waking because they're good markers of poor
asthma control of course frequent use of ventolin or
blue puffer is a marker again of poor asthma
control that can generally be much improved with good care
so we're talking here when you talk about ventolin or salbutamol
you're talking about what's called a reliever it doesn't treat the asthma it
just opens up the airways? That's it, yes. It's a temporary stopgap solution, but unfortunately
relied on by too many people in our community as the core treatment for their asthma. Indeed,
this week, in fact. In fact, this morning, new statistics come out showed that there were 3
million prescriptions for Ventolin in the last 12 months. So that's a lot of people sucking on
Ventolin. Despite all our efforts, it's still very heavily used. And we just have had for
decades better ways to manage asthma we haven't been able to effectively and consistently roll
them out although asthma deaths have gone down in australia and that's one of the really fascinating
things so we've dramatically reduced asthma deaths in our community so but we haven't got good current
symptom control improved to the same degree and it's one of the conundrums you know there clearly
are people in the community at risk of dying from asthma one presumes they're taking enough of their
core asthma treatment to avert very severe asthma and deaths in the majority of cases,
but are still tolerating a level of asthma symptom control that we think they don't need
to tolerate and does still put them at risk of some significant asthma crisis.
So what are the numbers?
In what proportion?
Yes.
So the core number that we worry about is people who, by standard criteria, have poorly
controlled asthma.
So we know around 25% of all people in Australia with asthma surveyed well have uncontrolled
asthma symptoms and are not taking a regular asthma preventer or, if you like, a solution
puffer for their asthma.
So that's one group of 25%.
Separately, there's 20% who report that they're using their core asthma treatment or preventer,
but they still have poorly controlled asthma.
As typified by the sort of symptoms that you were talking about a moment ago.
Sorry, I missed that one, Norman.
As typified by the sort of symptoms you were talking about a minute ago.
Correct.
And we've also had on the health report, but some time ago,
research which suggests that when people have given it...
So first of all, people think they grow out of asthma when they're adults,
which in fact is not true.
They grow out of it.
Some grow out of it in children,
but you don't grow out of it when you're an adult.
if you have established asthma in adult life spontaneous resolution is extraordinarily rare
and but there is research which suggests when you're not feeling too bad about your asthma
you think you haven't got it anymore it's only when you've got an asthma attack you think you've
got asthma yeah and and this is the problem of terminology that we you know a nut we haven't
quite cracked that uh that uh some people would describe or some people living with asthma would
describe an asthma attack as when their Ventolin doesn't work or relieve their symptoms as quickly
as they would expect it to, whereas we think the very need for Ventolin is a marker of poor asthma
control and it is in itself an asthma attack and something that we should worry about.
So getting a common language, a common terminology, a common way of approaching the goals of asthma
care is something we're still striving to achieve. So in other words, up to 40 or 50% of people with
asthma are on a bit of a knife edge and therefore when something like this thunderstorm asthma
event comes along they're hit particularly hard correct and some of the 20 who have uncontrolled
symptoms despite using their regular puffer appropriately may have symptoms for other
reasons they may report breathlessness because they're not as fit as they'd like to be
but uh but within that group there'll be there will be um uh people with asthma who are genuinely
they're at risk because they might be using their inhaler very badly. And that in itself is a signal
to some of the things that we can do, just simple attention to detail in taking treatment regularly,
in taking their inhalers with the correct technique so delivery is good and effect is maximised.
So just take us through the solutions here. So we've got all these complicated terminologies
like relievers, preventers and so on. What is the evidence-based treatment for asthma that's
that you're using your blue puffer too often, you've got these symptoms,
what is the evidence-based treatment?
Well, at the very least, patients, I shouldn't call them patients,
that's not dogma, people living with asthma who have regular symptoms
and are on no regular preventer treatment or core asthma treatment
should be taking one that includes an inhaled steroid component.
and just the administration of a relatively tiny dose
of inhaled steroid regularly virtually eliminates the risk
of asthma death and asthma crises, trips to hospital.
So that's the core.
That should be taken in an inhaler that the patient is familiar with
and they have good technique and one would expect
that their symptoms, breathless, cough, wheeze,
chest tightness will improve well.
Where they don't improve well, then sometimes a long-acting form of Ventolin or similar needs to be added.
Matthew, thank you very much indeed.
It's a great pleasure.
Matthew Peters is Professor of Respiratory Medicine at Macquarie University in Sydney.
And you're listening to The Health Report here on RN, ABC News Radio and CBC Radio across Canada.
A paper in the Canadian Medical Association Journal has issued a warning about an interaction between a blood thinner called dabigatran
and two cholesterol medications, statins.
one of which, lovastatin, isn't used in Australia, but the other, simvastatin, has been popular in the past.
The interaction increases the risk of a hemorrhage.
The lead author on the paper was pharmacist and clinical epidemiologist,
Associate Professor Tony Antoniu of the University of Toronto.
Dabigatrin, by the way, is used to prevent stroke in people with what's called atrial fibrillation.
That's correct. It's a blood thinner that's used by patients mostly with atrial fibrillation,
which is a kind of irregular heart rhythm.
and has become quite popular.
I mean, there's been a lot of controversy about dabigatrin
because it's not reversible and there's no test to really work out how well it's going.
That's correct, yeah.
But although the use of it has been increasing quite a bit,
I mean, during the period of our study,
the use of the drug had increased 90-fold between 2012 and 2014.
So despite some of the concerns with the drug, uptake was quite rapid.
And what made you think that statins, or at least these two statins we're talking about,
increase the risk of hemorrhage or might increase the risk of hemorrhage?
We thought about that because there was some previous research that had been done by others
that was sort of basic pharmacology type research that suggested that those two statins in particular,
lovastatin and simvastatin, had some properties that could increase the amount of the bigger
trend that was absorbed by our bodies and thereby then increase the risk of bleeding.
So what we were interested in examining was whether those findings from those other researchers
could translate into something important at the population level.
So what did you do in this study?
So what we did was we used Ontario's administrative health records,
and we started off by looking at all people who were 66 years of age and over
who had been prescribed a bigger trend between May 2012 and March 2014.
And then we just basically looked at people who had had either a stroke
or people who had been admitted to the hospital, had an emergency department room visit for bleed.
And then we took a look to see if there was a difference in the risk of either of these outcomes
according to the type of statin that patients were prescribed.
And why did you look at stroke?
Oh, I'm sorry.
We also looked at stroke because there is some evidence also that those same two statins,
lovastatin and simvastatin, could actually interfere with the way the bigotrin is activated
or turned on so that it would be a less effective blood thinner and therefore also then increase
the risk of stroke potentially.
So we actually did two separate studies.
Remembering, of course, that it's treating atrial fibrillation, which is the top chamber of your heart, where a clot can gather because it's not beating properly.
That's correct. So the clot can gather, form in the heart, and then travel to the brain and cause a stroke.
So we were thinking that if these two drugs decreased or interfered with the activation of the bigotran to its active form, they could interfere with its ability to prevent a clot.
And so these patients might also be at higher risk for stroke.
What did you find?
We actually found that there was no influence of lovastatin and simvastatin at all on the risk of stroke compared with other statins.
But in contrast, we found that being treated with simvastatin and lovastatin increased the risk of bleeding by about 40% or so relative to patients receiving one of the other statins.
Now, when you said major bleeding, what are we talking about here?
Yeah, that's an important question because we define major bleeding as any episode of a bleed that resulted in either a hospital admission or an emergency department room visit for bleeding.
About two-thirds, 70% of the bleeds we found were from the stomach.
So they were gastrointestinal bleeds, with a much smaller minority being brain bleeds.
And did anybody die as a result?
We didn't actually look at if anybody died, actually.
So I couldn't answer that question, if there were any deaths from the bleeds.
And you looked at the other statins, and you found that this risk did not exist?
Yeah, so we did this using those statins as the reference group,
And we did that because, or as a control group, because those statins don't have those same properties as lovastatin and simvastatin.
So we wouldn't expect them to behave in the same way when it comes to the way the bigotran is handled by the body.
Now I'm doing this story because it's an important public health message.
Today there's been a release in Australia of the top 10 drugs by numbers and by cost and so on.
And the top statins in Australia are atorvastatin, the trade name is Libitor, and rosuvastatin, the trade name is Crestor.
And while simvastatin and lovastatin were popular a few years ago, they're not anymore,
or simvastatin in particular, I should say.
Is it the same in Canada that they're not very popular drugs anymore?
Simvastatin is still used occasionally, but I would say the same is true up here.
Torvastatin and rosuvastatin have probably eclipsed the use of those other two drugs
for managing most patients.
But the core message here is that if you're on dabigatran and you're on a statin,
just check what statin it is just in case it's one of these two, simvastatin or lovastatin.
I think that would be the core message.
I think first not to do anything without consulting your physician, obviously.
But for people who are on the bigger trend,
I think our findings suggest that preferential use of one of the other statins
should probably be considered to derive the same benefits from statins
while minimizing the risk of a bleed.
Tony Antonio, thank you for joining us on the health report.
Thank you very much for your time and your interest.
Pharmacist and clinical epidemiologist,
Associate Professor Tony Antonio is at University of Toronto.
And remember, the interaction does just seem to be with Simvastatin.
and if you're living in Canada, lovastatin, not the other statins, and talk to your GP about it.
Now, a paper published in the prestigious American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology
has revealed an 8% reduction in preterm births from a preterm birth prevention initiative in Western Australia.
8% doesn't sound like a lot, but it is when you consider the impact that preterm birth has on community health,
particularly in disadvantaged populations.
One of the people involved in pioneering this initiative is Professor John Newnham of King
Edward Memorial Hospital and the Women's and Children's Infant Research Foundation in Perth.
Welcome to the Health Report, John.
Good afternoon, Norman. Thank you.
What do we know about the causes of preterm birth?
Well, preterm birth just describes birth at an age before 37 completed weeks. So it's really a
timing definition, the causes are multiple. There are multiple causes of preterm birth and they
differ at the different ages. So it's the range between 20 weeks and 37 weeks. The very early ones
we think are more often related to inflammation and infection. And later on, they're more related
to just spontaneous early onset of labor, which we don't understand. And sometimes because doctors
have pulled babies out early for one reason or another. Yes, we talked about that in the health
report before, there is an iatrogenic element to preterm birth. But you focused on hormones here.
No, we focused on the whole range. So the initiative that we launched two years ago
had six primary interventions, of which two or three were the major areas of work.
So firstly, we concentrated on the length of the cervix in mid-pregnancy.
So we now know that if you measure the length of the cervix in mid-pregnancy at the time
of your routine mid-pregnancy ultrasound scan, which in Australia is done at 18 weeks gestation,
the length of the cervix predicts heavily when you're going to deliver.
So a very short cervix or shortened cervix predicts early birth and a long cervix predicts
a later term birth.
and we now have relatively simple treatment that can markedly reduce that risk.
How reliable is that number?
Because women can be short, women can be tall
and presumably their cervix varies according to their body shape and size.
There's a small influence on the woman's height
but as a general rule, we have very strong cut-off.
So on an internal scan, a measurement of 25mm is our cut-off
and under that, the risk of preterm birth goes up dramatically.
Simply because the cervix is unlikely to hold the baby as the baby gets larger?
No, as you start getting uterine activity, which of course, for which there are no symptoms,
the woman's not aware of it, it starts pulling the cervix up and thinning it,
which normally occurs towards term and in labor.
But in mid-pregnancy and women at risk of going into preterm labor,
this starts happening silently much earlier.
So what do you do about it?
Well, we've got several options available to us.
The first thing is you need to know it's there so the woman can have this discussed with her.
We have vaginal progesterone treatment, which is a natural hormone available in a pessary,
one pessary, one tablet basically, in the vagina each night,
and that reduces the risk of preterm birth by about a half.
And it's safe for the baby?
We believe it's safe for the baby.
We, it's been in use, progesterone's been in use for about 50 years, one way or another.
we need better safety data going well into childhood
but at the moment it's natural vaginal progesterone
and we're operating on the assumption at the moment that it's safe
and also if the cervix is super short
then there are surgical interventions that you can do
yeah so if the cervix is very short
if it's surprisingly short
we have available to us as we have had for quite a long time
the idea of surgically closing the cervix
And then women with a history of preterm birth can get progesterone on a regular basis.
That's one of your other interventions.
Yes.
So women who've had a previous preterm birth before, in particular an early one, whether
it be spontaneous labor or if the membrane's ruptured, if we prescribe progesterone, this
progesterone treatment starting at 16 weeks of pregnancy, our evidence is that that will
halve the risk of recurrence.
and you've got a warning for doctors,
don't deliver a baby under 38 weeks unless you really have to.
Yeah, so we also had a major push across Western Australia
starting in mid-2014 to make sure that no one delivered a baby
before 38 and a half weeks at least
without a solid medical or pregnancy indication to do so.
So social delivery or unnecessary delivery before that time
was something we were working very heavily against.
And what we've done, which has been unique,
is that instead of targeting just doctors,
we targeted the doctors, the midwives,
all healthcare professionals,
and the women and the families of Western Australia
through a print and social media campaign.
And smoking?
Smoking, yes.
Smoking's a major risk factor for preterm birth.
The smoking rate in pregnancy in Western Australia and Australia
has fallen down to about 12%, but we've got a lot of work to do because in Aboriginal Australians,
the smoking messages have not worked and their smoking rate in pregnancy sits at about 50%.
It's been unchanged for the last 20 years. That's an area in which we've got more work to do in the
future. And you've got one preterm birth delivery clinic that's specialising in this area for the
state. Yeah. So we started at, we only have one tertiary level perinatal centre in Western
Australia. That's at King Edward Memorial Hospital. And we started a dedicated clinic.
The clinic is heavily based on measuring the length of the cervix and providing appropriate
treatment. It's not a big clinic. We aim to provide a backstop, a final point of referral
for very complicated cases. But essentially, if you're living in Geraldton, you'd expect the
obstetrician or the GP to manage this in Geraldton? Well, a lot of women will either call and will
give them a management plan over the telephone with instructions for the doctors out there,
or they'll come down for one or two visits and they'll go back home with their management plan.
Now, these great plans often fall over in implementation. I mean, this sounds like a
massive project. Well, it was, but it was done by a small number of people. So the most important
thing we needed to do was to get the message out across all of Western Australia. Western Australia
is ideal for this. It's a medical island with desert to the right and ocean to the left.
We have one tertiary level centre, so everybody knows each other, everybody relates to each other.
So we put together an outreach team consisting of myself, a junior obstetrician, our chief ultrasound imaging person, and one or two of our specialty midwives.
And we, over a period of 15, 16 months, did a lap of Western Australia.
We travelled more than 14,000 kilometres and we ran evening workshops.
More than 500 healthcare practitioners attended these workshops in their own hospitals so that we knew that everybody knew exactly what this plan was.
So can it work in New South Wales or Victoria where big hospitals don't talk to each other and compete with each other?
Well, we hope to spread this out.
Now we've demonstrated in Western Australia it's worked.
We hope now to spread this out over into Eastern Australia.
And that's my work for 2017.
And it's affordable?
Well, it's actually very cheap.
So the clinic, the dedicated new clinic,
was funded by the Minister for Health on a block grant
and the business case that we presented to the minister
showed that the entire clinical service would be paid in a year
by just preventing two early preterm births.
So that's very easy to demonstrate.
Then the outreach program actually doesn't cost very much money
but it was funded by philanthropy.
So, you know, the McCuskers and Nicola and Andrew Forrest
and all through the Women and Infants Research Foundation funded it.
But actually, it does not cost much money.
The media helped.
We won prizes in a thing called the Orange Seed Competition.
And so the West did a lot of free advertising for us.
And we use social media, of course, which is free.
So we look forward to the national spread.
John Newman, congratulations, and thank you for joining us on the Health Report.
Thank you very much, Norman.
John Newman is founder and chair of the WA Preterm Birth Initiative
and Executive Director of the Women and Infants Research Foundation in Perth.
Work done at the University of Aberdeen in Scotland
has developed for modern IVF treatment
what they think is quite a reliable predictor of the chances of a live birth,
a very controversial topic.
On the line from Aberdeen is the lead author of this paper,
Dr David McLernan, who's Research Fellow in Medical Statistics.
Welcome to the Health Report.
Hi Norman, nice to speak to you.
What are the elements of the prediction here?
Okay, so what we did was we developed two novel online calculators.
The first one uses information from the couple that's available before they actually start IVF,
such as the age of the woman and the diagnosis of their fertility problem.
We use that to predict their overall chance of having a baby over an entire package of IVF treatment.
and then there's a second calculator which then updates these predictions
using further information which is available at the first attempt
such as the number of eggs that were collected
and the number of embryos that were transferred.
And of course what's called cryopreservation
because there's increasing evidence which is not there in other predictors
which is that frozen embryos seem to do better than fresh embryos.
Yes, sorry.
We also included acquired preservation status of embryos.
There are quite a few trials going on globally at the minute
to compare the effect of fresh and frozen embryo transfers.
I think one or two of them have results already
that show that the live birth rates are no worse with frozen embryos.
So just take us through some of these factors in your calculator.
So a woman's age.
You compared a woman who's aged 31 versus 37.
Yeah, well, yes.
That was only to present the result in a clear manner.
We used all women's ages.
I'm sure, but this is an example so people can hook on to it.
Yes, yes.
So if you were 31 versus 37, your chances were 66% better
just for being a bit younger.
Yes.
We all know that the effect of women's age on the chances of having a baby declined from around the age of 30 onwards.
And they get worse from about 35 to 50.
And duration of infertility pre-treatment also had a predictive value?
Yes.
So obviously the longer you've been trying to get pregnant, the lower your chances of having a baby.
What about post-treatment predictors?
So the number of eggs collected?
Yes, so we showed that the more eggs that you've collected in your first IVF attempt
increase your chances of having a baby up until around 13, 14 eggs.
At that point, your chances actually stay quite steady with further eggs.
And having a frozen embryo makes a huge difference.
Yes.
Almost doubles your chances.
It does, yes.
That's just a marker of the quality of the embryos that the woman has.
So the more embryos you have that are top quality,
the more chance of having enough left over after your fresh embryo transfer to freeze to use later on.
Now, you illustrate this with a case study.
So one is pre-treatment, a 30-year-old woman with two years of unexplained infertility.
What are her chances?
Okay.
So we showed that her chance of having a baby over one after the first complete cycle of IVF is 46%.
And over three complete cycles, it's 79%.
And when we say complete cycle, we're including all embryo transfer attempts
from that one episode of ovarian stimulation.
And the stage at which the embryo is transferred also makes a difference.
So then if she has a fresh embryo cycle, it drops considerably.
If she has a fresh embryo?
So her chances almost halve.
You talk about when she's run out of embryos and there's no freezing,
then the chances drop quite dramatically.
Yes, it's because she hasn't got enough frozen embryos left in order to actually carry on to increase her chances.
It's all cumulative effect that we're measuring here with this model.
So if you've only got one fresh embryo, your chances are quite low.
So what about the male partner? You've assumed that that's constant, there's no problem with the male partner.
Yes, unfortunately the data that we use, the national data from the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority,
which is the regulatory body for IVF treatment in the UK,
didn't include factors on the male.
Apart from perhaps the actual diagnosis of infertility,
if it was a male factor problem, we were able to include that information.
And you didn't include intracytoplasmic sperm injection,
which is almost universal in the Australian context.
We actually did include that as well in the model.
But it didn't make a difference?
Yeah, well, in the post-tribal model, it showed that XC was just very...
XC, sorry, is an intracetoplasmic sperm injection where they inject the sperm into the egg.
We showed it was just marginally, had a slightly lower effect compared to IVF.
Interesting.
So time will tell whether this applies to the Australian context.
Lots more questions to ask, but unfortunately we've run out of time.
Thanks very much for joining us.
Okay, thanks.
Dr David McLernan, who's a research fellow in medical statistics at the University of Aberdeen, my alma mater.
I'm Norman Swan. You've been listening to The Health Report. Please join me next week.
From the founder of Apple to comedian Andy Samberg,
from the head of Netflix to the man who built the World Wide Web,
from the creators of the record-breaking podcast Serial
to start-ups that are breaking ground right here in Australia,
if you want to hear from the movers and the shakers,
media, technology and culture around Australia and the globe,
there is literally one show.
It also happens to be the most literally named show.
